chapter: Kansas City rooms and Piney Brown
title: Ellis Burton, the Yellow Front owner who fed musicians
summary: Goodwin describes Burton as a strict, generous Black owner who cooked big feasts for musicians and let them jam after hours.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Crook, I'm sure you've had memories of the Yellow Front. Would you tell us something about it, what you were doing there?

What I remember about the Yellow Front was the gentleman that run the Yellow Front, Ellis Burton. He was a friend to the musicians, a very good friend. If you would go by Ellis Burton and you were kind of low on cash, the musicians that he liked so well, he would always replenish them.
Was he white or black, Crook?

He was a black man and he understood operating a nightclub and he ruled with an iron hand. Whenever he would speak, I don't care what would be going on in the club, well they would cool down if Ellis would come around. He would run the joint. He kept law and order, but above all, he was a great guy and he would -- he would feed the musicians; he would cook up a big pot of spaghetti or just what have you, you know, --
-- some kind of stew or gumbo or just anything and just invite us, the guys who were playing casual in town on engagements, well invite a big bunch of them down and --

-- after we finished hours, we'd all have a big feast. He's set a big, long table and boy, we would go at it. You know, all you want to drink, all you want to eat. He would do this several times a year.
Well, did you play then too, after hours down there?
Oh yeah, every night practically we'd all go by as a sort of a tribute to him. We would jam in the joint, you know, until the wee hours of the morning whenever we had a chance to do it, you know.
I would guess then you jammed with Baby's band down there?
